The mechanism is a tagging scheme. Types that JSON can't represent are wrapped in a one-key dict, such as `{" t": [...]}`, on write and unwrapped on read.

- **`src/tessel/sessions.py`**
  - `SignedCookieSessionInterface` is the default session interface. Its `serializer` attribute (line 300) is the module-level `session_json_serializer = TypedCookieSerializer()` (line 273). Line 316 passes that serializer into the signing serializer, so the cookie payload is signed and goes through the tagging step.
  - `SignedCookieSession` is the session object itself.
- **`src/tessel/json/tag.py`**
  - `TypedCookieSerializer` (line 219) holds the ordered list of tag classes, built from `default_tags` (line 238). `dumps` and `loads` call `tag()` and `untag()`. `register()` adds custom tags.
  - `TypeMarker` (line 60) is the base class for the tag classes. Each one implements `to_json()` and `to_python()`, and also decides whether it applies to a value and which tag key it uses.
  - `TagTuple` (line 133) turns a tuple into a list of tagged items and back into a tuple.
  - `TagBytes` (line 159) encodes bytes as text and decodes them back.
  - `TagDateTime` (line 205) turns a datetime into a string and parses it back.
  - Other markers: `TagDict` and `PassDict` (dicts), `PassList`, `TagMarkup`, and `TagUUID`.

`TagDict` escapes user dicts that happen to look like a tag by renaming the key to `<key>__`. That stops them from being misread as tagged values on load.

I read the grep results but not the method bodies, so I haven't checked how `dumps` and `loads` walk the value or how each tag matches its type.
